5. Recognition lab

Read the stem pattern, commit to a diagnosis, then reveal the discriminator.

Pattern: local URI symptoms, minimal systemic illness, most common cold virus.
Rhinovirus. Think common cold + ICAM-1 + non-enveloped +ssRNA.
Pattern: fatigue for weeks, severe sore throat, posterior cervical nodes, splenomegaly.
EBV mononucleosis. Monospot/atypical lymphocytes; avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin rash trap.
Pattern: bilateral jaw swelling + orchitis in an unvaccinated young adult.
Mumps. Respiratory entry → viremia → systemic organ spread.
Pattern: cough + coryza + conjunctivitis + Koplik spots, then facial rash spreading downward.
Measles. Remember pneumonia and SSPE as complications.
Pattern: abrupt dry cough, weakness/fatigue, seasonal winter illness; concern for post-viral bacterial pneumonia.
Influenza. Segmented −ssRNA; HA attaches, NA releases; drift vs shift.
Pattern: infant with wheeze, crackles, tachypnea, air trapping/hyperinflation ± apnea.
RSV bronchiolitis. F protein → fusion/syncytia; no viremia; reinfection common.
Pattern: young child with barky cough and inspiratory stridor.
Parainfluenza croup. Look for the steeple sign.
Pattern: respiratory infection progresses to diffuse lung injury, hypoxia, inflammatory/coagulation complications.
Severe COVID-19. In the lecture: hypoxia is the key trigger for dexamethasone.

8. Printable exam sheet

Part I — Core framework + must-know virology

Master classification: Rhinovirus = non-enveloped +ssRNA Picornaviridae. Adenovirus = non-enveloped dsDNA. EBV = enveloped dsDNA herpesvirus. Influenza = enveloped segmented −ssRNA Orthomyxoviridae. RSV/hMPV = enveloped nonsegmented −ssRNA Pneumoviridae. Parainfluenza/mumps/measles = enveloped −ssRNA paramyxovirus family group. Coronavirus = enveloped +ssRNA.

Normal-to-abnormal bridge

RuleExam use
+ssRNA can function as mRNA.Can be translated quickly after entering cytoplasm.
−ssRNA cannot be translated directly.Must carry polymerase to make a complementary readable strand.
Most RNA viruses replicate in cytoplasm.Influenza is the exception emphasized here: nucleus.
Most DNA viruses replicate in nucleus.EBV and adenovirus fit the DNA-virus framework.
Envelope = lipid bilayer.More labile to heat/detergents/alcohol; close-contact/droplet spread emphasized.
Non-enveloped = naked capsid.More resistant in environment; fomites matter (rhinovirus, adenovirus).

Clinical-syndrome decoder

If the stem gives…Think first…Then confirm with…
Simple common coldRhinovirus+ssRNA, non-enveloped, ICAM-1, many serotypes, supportive care.
Cold/URI + conjunctivitis or broad systemic manifestationsAdenovirusdsDNA, non-enveloped, fecal-oral/fomite potential.
Weeks of fatigue + severe pharyngitis + posterior cervical nodes/spleenEBVMonospot, atypical lymphocytes, dsDNA enveloped, B-cell latency.
Parotitis + orchitisMumps−ssRNA enveloped, viremia, MMR.
4 C’s + descending maculopapular rashMeaslesKoplik spots, pneumonia/SSPE, MMR.
Abrupt systemic respiratory illnessInfluenza8 segments, nucleus, HA/NA, drift/shift, post-viral bacterial pneumonia.
Infant bronchiolitis ± apneaRSVF protein/syncytia, no viremia, reinfection common.
RSV-like bronchiolitis but “second most common”hMPVPneumoviridae, supportive care.
Barky cough + inspiratory stridorParainfluenzaCroup, steeple sign, 6 months–4 years.
Seasonal cold vs SARS/MERS/COVID severe diseaseCoronavirusEnveloped +ssRNA; use clinical context to distinguish subtype.

Influenza — the dense part

Genome
8-segment −ssRNA, enveloped, Orthomyxoviridae.
Location
Only RNA virus in this lecture that replicates in the nucleus.
HA
Attachment/penetration; binds sialic acid.
NA
Release of new virions. Inhibitors → block viral exit.
Drift
Point mutations → gradual antigenic change → epidemics.
Shift
Segment reassortment → abrupt major antigenic change → pandemic potential.
Trap: “post-influenza bacterial pneumonia” can tempt you to answer Staph aureus automatically. The professor clarified that Strep pneumoniae is still the most common, while Staph aureus has the special classic association.

RSV — what actually separates it

FeatureExam interpretation
F proteinFusion + syncytium formation; major mechanistic/prevention target.
InfantsMost common severe lower-respiratory disease / bronchiolitis.
ApneaImportant infant presentation.
No viremiaSpread is along respiratory epithelium.
Reinfection commonNatural infection does not give durable sterilizing immunity.
TreatmentSupportive care is current lecture emphasis.
Lecture/practice discrepancy: the legacy practice question’s key uses ribavirin. The professor’s current transcript says she “should have taken aerosolized ribavirin out” and tells the class to cross it out. For studying this lecture, prioritize supportive care; if the exact old practice item appears unchanged, know that its key says ribavirin.

Part II — Distinctions, traps, and reverse reasoning

Easy-to-confuse pairShared featureBest discriminator
Rhinovirus vs adenovirusNon-enveloped respiratory viruses; fomitesRhinovirus = +ssRNA + common cold/ICAM-1. Adenovirus = dsDNA + conjunctivitis/systemic range.
Influenza vs parainfluenzaEnveloped −ssRNA; HA/NA languageInfluenza = segmented + nucleus + drift/shift. Parainfluenza = nonsegmented + cytoplasm + croup.
RSV vs hMPVPneumoviridae, bronchiolitisRSV = #1 and F-protein/syncytia emphasis; hMPV = #2 in winter–spring.
Mumps vs measlesParamyxovirus group, enveloped −ssRNA, MMR-preventableMumps = parotitis/orchitis/systemic viremia. Measles = 4 C’s + rash + SSPE.
Seasonal coronavirus vs severe coronavirusesEnveloped +ssRNA coronavirusRoutine strains → common cold; SARS/MERS/SARS-CoV-2 → severe pneumonia/systemic complications.

“What happens next?” chains

Viral URI → epithelial damage → impaired clearance → secondary bacterial infection.
Influenza NA inhibited → virions cannot efficiently release → viral spread/replication reduced.
RSV F-protein fusion → cell-to-cell spread/syncytia → bronchiolar disease.
Parainfluenza upper-airway inflammation → subglottic narrowing → stridor + barky cough + steeple sign.
COVID delayed control → DAMP/inflammatory escalation → tissue injury + coagulation activation → microthrombi/ARDS.
Influenza genome segmentation → reassortment possible → antigenic shift.

Rapid treatment/prevention logic

VirusLecture treatment emphasisPrevention
RhinovirusSupportiveHand hygiene; no vaccine.
AdenovirusUsually supportive; severe immunocompromised cases may use specific antiviralsHand hygiene; live oral vaccine only for military recruits.
EBVSupportive; avoid ampicillin/amoxicillin rash trapNo vaccine listed.
Mumps / measlesSupportive; vitamin A for measles complication reductionMMR.
InfluenzaNA inhibitors; baloxavirAnnual vaccine.
RSVSupportiveAdult vaccines; maternal vaccine or infant monoclonal antibody strategies.
hMPV / parainfluenzaSupportive / syndrome managementNo vaccine in lecture.
COVID-19Risk/severity-based antiviral + anti-inflammatory approachUpdated vaccine strategy from lecture.
